ALCINA — Survival analyses

HES-1, circulating tumor cells and circulating tumor DNA

Author

Alexandre Sitbon

Published

September 1, 2026

Objectives

The objective of this analysis was to investigate the association between baseline HES-1 expression, circulating tumor cells (CTC), circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), and survival outcomes.

The analyses correspond to the questions requested by Quentin:

  1. Description of the distribution of nuclear and cytoplasmic HES-1 H-scores.
  2. Association between nuclear and cytoplasmic H-scores and progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), considering H-score as a continuous variable.
  3. Association between nuclear H-score categories (<100 versus >200) and PFS and OS.
  4. Association between baseline CTC count and PFS and OS.
  5. Association between baseline ctDNA level and PFS and OS.
  6. Association between ctDNA clearance at T2 and PFS and OS.

Data import and quality control

The dataset contained one row per patient. PFS and OS were expressed in days. Event indicators were coded as 1 for an observed event and 0 for a censored observation.

No missing value was imputed.

Patients PFS events PFS censored OS events OS censored
24 19 5 13 11

Expected values are 24 patients, 9 PFS events and 13 OS events.

2. HES-1 H-score as a continuous variable and survival

Question from Quentin:
“Could you evaluate PFS and OS according to H-score, considering H-score as a continuous variable?”

Statistical analysis

Nuclear and cytoplasmic HES-1 H-scores were analyzed separately using univariable Cox proportional hazards models.

For easier interpretation, H-scores were divided by 100. Hazard ratios therefore represent the change in hazard associated with a 100-point increase in H-score.

Afficher le code R 
cox_nuc_pfs <- coxph(
  Surv(pfs_days, pfs_event) ~ hscore_nuc_100,
  data = df
)

cox_nuc_os <- coxph(
  Surv(os_days, os_event) ~ hscore_nuc_100,
  data = df
)

cox_cyto_pfs <- coxph(
  Surv(pfs_days, pfs_event) ~ hscore_cyto_100,
  data = df
)

cox_cyto_os <- coxph(
  Surv(os_days, os_event) ~ hscore_cyto_100,
  data = df
)

Results

Outcome Predictor Scale N Events HR [95% CI] p-value
PFS Nuclear H-score +100 points 21 18 1.54 [0.94–2.53] 0.087
OS Nuclear H-score +100 points 21 12 1.22 [0.70–2.10] 0.483
PFS Cytoplasmic H-score +100 points 21 18 1.43 [0.64–3.22] 0.384
OS Cytoplasmic H-score +100 points 21 12 1.56 [0.62–3.93] 0.341

A HR greater than 1 indicates a higher hazard associated with increasing H-score, whereas a HR below 1 indicates a lower hazard.

3. Nuclear HES-1 H-score categories and survival

Question from Quentin:
“For nuclear H-score, patients with an H-score <100 were classified as low and patients with an H-score >200 as high.”

Statistical analysis

Only nuclear H-score was categorized.

  • Low nuclear H-score: <100
  • High nuclear H-score: >200

Patients with values between 100 and 200 were excluded from this categorical comparison.

PFS and OS were estimated using Kaplan-Meier survival curves and compared using the log-rank test. Cox regression was used to estimate the hazard ratio for High versus Low H-score.

4. Baseline circulating tumor cells and survival

Question from Quentin:
“Could you also evaluate PFS and OS according to CTC at inclusion?”

Statistical analysis

Baseline CTC status was analyzed as a binary variable. Patients with a CTC value equal to 0 were classified as CTC absent, whereas patients with a CTC value greater than 0 were classified as CTC present. Patients with missing baseline CTC data were excluded from this analysis.

PFS and OS were compared according to baseline CTC status using Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank tests, and univariable Cox proportional hazards models.

5. Baseline circulating tumor DNA and survival

Question from Quentin:
“Could you perform the same analysis using circulating tumor DNA?”

Statistical analysis

Baseline ctDNA was analyzed as a continuous variable using separate univariable Cox proportional hazards models for PFS and OS.

For easier interpretation, ctDNA values were divided by 100. Hazard ratios therefore represent a 100-unit increase in baseline ctDNA.

Afficher le code R 
cox_ctdna_pfs <- coxph(
  Surv(pfs_days, pfs_event) ~ ctdna_t1_100,
  data = df
)

cox_ctdna_os <- coxph(
  Surv(os_days, os_event) ~ ctdna_t1_100,
  data = df
)

Results

Outcome Predictor Scale N Events HR [95% CI] p-value
PFS Baseline ctDNA +100 units 24 19 1.02 [0.99–1.05] 0.221
OS Baseline ctDNA +100 units 24 13 1.04 [1.00–1.07] 0.028

6. ctDNA clearance at T2 and survival

Question from Quentin:
“Could you also evaluate survival according to clearance of circulating tumor DNA at T2, i.e. patients with no remaining ctDNA (value 0) versus the others?”

Statistical analysis

Patients with a T2 ctDNA value equal to 0 were classified as having ctDNA clearance.

Patients with a T2 ctDNA value greater than 0 were classified as having no clearance.

Patients with missing T2 ctDNA were excluded.

Statistical interpretation

These analyses are exploratory and univariable.

The PFS analysis includes only 9 events in the complete cohort. Consequently, confidence intervals may be wide and estimates should be interpreted primarily according to their magnitude and precision rather than according to statistical significance alone.

ANALYSES COMPLEMENTAIRES

The following complementary analyses were performed following additional requests.

1. 95% confidence intervals for median PFS and OS

Question: “Could you provide 95% confidence intervals for PFS and OS?”

Statistical analysis

Median progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method.
95% confidence intervals are reported whenever estimable. Because of the limited sample size and number of events, one or both confidence interval limits may not be estimable.

Median progression-free and overall survival
Kaplan–Meier estimates with 95% confidence intervals
Outcome N Events Median survival 95% CI
Progression-free survival 24 19 334 days (11.0 months) 183–792 days
Overall survival 24 13 563 days (18.5 months) 491–NA days

Interpretation

Median survival estimates should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited sample size.
When a confidence interval boundary cannot be estimated, it is reported as NA rather than being replaced or extrapolated.

3. Corrected analysis of ctDNA clearance at T2

Question: “Patients without detectable ctDNA at baseline cannot experience ctDNA clearance. Patients 15, 19 and 46 should therefore be excluded from the clearance analysis.”

Statistical analysis

ctDNA clearance was evaluated only among patients with detectable ctDNA at baseline (T1).

Patients were classified as:

  • Clearance: detectable ctDNA at T1 followed by ctDNA = 0 at T2.
  • No clearance: detectable ctDNA at T1 and persistent detectable ctDNA at T2.

Patients with ctDNA = 0 at baseline were excluded because clearance cannot be defined in these patients.

4. Overall survival according to ctDNA at relapse (T4)

Question: “Could you evaluate overall survival according to ctDNA at relapse (T4), both as a continuous variable and as a binary variable (present versus absent)?”

Statistical analysis

Overall survival was evaluated from the T4 assessment using the dedicated survival variables.

ctDNA at T4 was analyzed:

  1. as a continuous variable using a univariable Cox proportional hazards model;
  2. as a binary variable, with ctDNA classified as absent when equal to 0 and present when greater than 0.

Patients with missing ctDNA at T4 or missing survival information were excluded.

Population included in the T4 analysis

Population included in the ctDNA T4 survival analysis
Patients Deaths Censored ctDNA absent ctDNA present
15 9 6 4 11

4.1. ctDNA at T4 as a continuous variable

Cox proportional hazards model

ctDNA at T4 was first analyzed as a continuous predictor of overall survival from T4.

For easier interpretation, ctDNA was divided by 100. The hazard ratio therefore represents the change in the hazard of death associated with a 100-unit increase in ctDNA at T4.

Afficher le code R 
df_t4 <- df_t4 |>
  mutate(
    ctdna_t4_100 = adntc_t4 / 100
  )

cox_ctdna_t4_continuous <- coxph(
  Surv(
    os_adntc_t4,
    event_t4
  ) ~ ctdna_t4_100,
  data = df_t4
)

Results

Association between ctDNA at T4 and overall survival
ctDNA analyzed as a continuous variable
Outcome Predictor Scale N Events HR [95% CI] p-value
OS from T4 ctDNA at T4 +100 units 15 9 1.03 [0.99–1.06] 0.134

A hazard ratio greater than 1 indicates an increasing hazard of death with increasing ctDNA at T4.

OS from T4 ctDNA at T4 Present vs Absent 15 9 841637513.40 [0.00–Inf] 0.999

Interpretation

The continuous analysis evaluates the association between increasing ctDNA levels at relapse and the subsequent hazard of death.

The binary analysis compares overall survival from T4 between patients with detectable and undetectable ctDNA at relapse.

Because this analysis is restricted to patients reaching T4 with available ctDNA measurements, the results should be considered exploratory. Effect sizes and their 95% confidence intervals should be interpreted alongside statistical significance.
